summary: Draws on the TISDAG project to outline an approach for integrating widely scattered directory servers into one service rather than mandating a single product.

plainLanguage.summary: Many separate directories can work together as one lookup service without forcing everyone to use the same software.

questions: how do integrated directory services work
subtitle: A modular gateway approach for integrating distributed directory services.

tldr.problem: Building a single, unified directory service across multiple independent servers and organizations is difficult. Different systems use different protocols and schemas.
tldr.mechanism: The TISDAG architecture inserts a coordinated set of gateway modules between clients and servers. Client Access Points handle incoming queries, Service Access Points proxy to remote servers, and all components communicate through a single internal protocol (DAG/IP).
tldr.outcome: Many different directory servers and protocols can be integrated into one unified service without forcing all servers to adopt the same software or protocol.

facts.label: Main components
facts.value: Client Access Points, Service Access Points, Internal Servers

today: RFC 2970 is an Informational document describing architectural principles from the TISDAG project and how they could apply to other query-response services. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Problem of Scattered Directory Services
sections.content:
Organizations across the world run their own directory services—whitepages databases, business registries, telephone directories. Each uses its own software and protocols. A user wanting a unified view of all this information cannot do it without buying one single expensive system from one vendor and convincing everyone else to switch to it.

The TISDAG project (Technical Infrastructure for Swedish Directory Access Gateways) tackled this problem by designing a gateway architecture. Rather than mandate a single protocol and schema for everyone, TISDAG inserted a layer of translation modules between clients and the scattered servers. This approach lets organizations keep their existing systems while still being part of a larger unified service.
sections.plainLanguage: If everyone used different phone books, an architecture that translates between them would let customers find people without everyone changing their phone book.

sections.title: The Gateway Architecture
sections.content:
The architecture has three main types of components. Client Access Points (CAPs) face outward and accept queries from client software. They handle one or more external protocols—LDAP, HTTP, Whois++. The CAP translates the client query into internal actions.

Service Access Points (SAPs) face outward toward remote servers. They translate internal queries into the protocols those servers speak and convert responses back. Internal Servers provide specialized services only to other components—such as a referral index that tells the system which remote servers might have information for a given query.

All internal components communicate using a single query-response protocol called DAG/IP. This means a CAP does not need to know how many SAPs exist or which protocol each one speaks. Configuration and routing happen behind the scenes.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine a help desk. Customers call in (CAP), help desk staff look things up in records (internal server), and contact other departments (SAPs) if needed. Everyone talks to the help desk in the same language, but each department outside speaks their own language.

sections.title: Key Design Principles
sections.content:
Four design principles guided TISDAG. First, the system needed to support multiple client and server protocols without change to the service itself. Second, queries and schemas other than the original ones should be supported as the service grows. Third, the architecture should be modular and reconfigurable—adding more servers or load-sharing should be easy.

Fourth, there is an inside and outside to the service. The world sees only the public CAPs. The referral service, lookup functions, and security mechanisms are internal components accessible only to other components. This separation of concerns lets each part evolve independently.
sections.plainLanguage: The design assumes that client protocols will change, that the service will grow, and that some information is secret. By separating the public face from the internal machinery, change becomes easier.

sections.title: Example Applications
sections.content:
The TISDAG project implemented a whitepages service with CAPs for HTTP, SMTP, Whois++, LDAPv2, and LDAPv3. Clients using any of these protocols see the same unified service. Behind the scenes, SAPs proxied to remote Whois++ and LDAP servers, and an internal referral index told each CAP which remote services might have the information.

The architecture extends to other services. An operator service for phone number portability could have CAPs for HTTP and wireless access. It would internally consult a lookup service to find which country issued the phone number, then query national services and finally the current carrier for details. A medical system could support a proprietary protocol for secure in-hospital terminals and a wireless protocol for roaming staff, with internal servers for authentication and a referral service to find records across hospitals.
sections.plainLanguage: Different services have different needs. Some need many protocols, some need to look things up in stages, some need heavy security. The architecture lets each service configure its own pieces without changing the basic framework.

sections.title: The DAG/IP Internal Protocol
sections.content:
DAG/IP is the glue binding the architecture together. Rather than build a heavyweight search protocol, DAG/IP is a lightweight query-response framework. It must support different query types, different result sets, and be flexible enough to carry security credentials, lookups, and capability negotiation.

The document proposes that DAG/IP should be more than just a query protocol. It should establish authenticated, secure connections and let components negotiate what transaction types and capabilities they support. This way, a new type of CAP or SAP can be added to the system without hardcoding knowledge into existing components.
sections.plainLanguage: DAG/IP is the language components use to talk to each other. It needs to be simple enough to stay lightweight but smart enough to handle security, lookups, and new service types.
